{"author": "person-ef78c9de", "body": "/kind bug

**What happened**:
Trying out snapshot build 20200928 with #3493. virtio-fs is setup to map a cephFS backed PVC.

Ubuntu 18.04. Host kernel: 5.4.0-47-generic. No SELinux. Apparmor enabled.

The `docker-default` AppArmor profile is too restrictive for Virtio-FS to work.

Qemu fails to start with:
```
{"component":"virt-launcher","level":"error","msg":"internal error: qemu unexpectedly closed the monitor: 2020-09-30T21:08:34.249505Z qemu-kvm: -device vhost-user-fs-pci,chardev=chr-vu-fs0,queue-size=1024,tag=sharedfs,bus=pci.1,addr=0x0: Failed to read msg header. Read 0 instead of 12. Original request 1.","pos":"qemuProcessReportLogError:2064","subcomponent":"libvirt","thread":"56","timestamp":"2020-09-30T21:08:34.250000Z"}
qemu-kvm: -device vhost-user-fs-pci,chardev=chr-vu-fs0,queue-size=1024,tag=sharedfs,bus=pci.1,addr=0x0: vhost_dev_init failed: Operation not permitted
```

virtiofsd logs:
```
[617100180193229] [ID: 00000001] mount(/, MS_REC|MS_SLAVE): Permission denied
[617101334792332] [ID: 00000194] virtio_session_mount: Waiting for vhost-user socket connection...
[617101363029043] [ID: 00000194] virtio_session_mount: Received vhost-user socket connection
[617101384956914] [ID: 00000001] mount(/, MS_REC|MS_SLAVE): Permission denied
[617102539847175] [ID: 00000205] virtio_session_mount: Waiting for vhost-user socket connection...
[617102575292582] [ID: 00000205] virtio_session_mount: Received vhost-user socket connection
[617102593016668] [ID: 00000001] mount(/, MS_REC|MS_SLAVE): Permission denied
[617103827655704] [ID: 00000216] virtio_session_mount: Waiting for vhost-user socket connection...
[617103856087607] [ID: 00000216] virtio_session_mount: Received vhost-user socket connection
[617103872973299] [ID: 00000001] mount(/, MS_REC|MS_SLAVE): Permission denied
```

**Workaround**
Annotate the VMI with:
```
      annotations:
        container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/compute: unconfined
```

Since new app armor profiles can't easily be created a reasonable fix to this bug is to have `virt-controller` add this annotation to the Pod. This _might_ fail if AppArmor is enabled in Kubernetes but the kernel module is not loaded. Test on a non-apparmor enabled system before merging a change like this. It should be included in the (hopefully upcoming) documentation for the Virtio-FS implementation at least.", "closed_by": null, "comments": [{"author": "person-ef78c9de", "body": "This is related to apparmor. I'm wondering what kind of host OS are you testing this on?
Also, there is an additional log file, that is not being collected right now that we can look at.
If you'd exec into the virt-launcher pod `kubectl exec -it [virt-launcher-pod-name] -c compute -n [namespace]` a virtiofsd log file will appear the moment it starts (it may take some time, depending on the infra) - please look in `/var/log/libvirt/qemu/[domain_name]-virtiofsd.log`", "body_missing": false, "created_at": "2020-10-01T11:21:05Z", "id": 702067364}, {"author": "person-1118c074", "body": "> This is related to apparmor. I’m running default apparmor settings for Kubernetes / Ubuntu / Docker so I would imagine anyone running Ubuntu on the host will have the same issue as me.", "body_missing": false, "created_at": "2020-10-01T12:30:50Z", "id": 702101574}, {"author": "person-ef78c9de", "body": "Adding `container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/compute: unconfined` on the pod spec should solve (or at least workaround) this.", "body_missing": false, "created_at": "2020-10-01T18:55:19Z", "id": 702332821}, {"author": "person-ef78c9de", "body": "@person-1118c074: I have confirmed that annotating the VMI with `unconfined` solves the problem. **Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?**:

> Uncomment only one, leave it on its own line:
>

/kind bug

> /kind enhancement


**What happened**:

The WFFC handling of PVCs right now involves first starting a pod without a VM inside which binds the WFFC PVCs to a node.
Then we hope that when we stop that pod and start the actual pod with a VM inside, that the pod can still fit on the node.

In case that a cluster is used well, this assumption is very likely pretty often false. Also our startup flow is pretty complicated due to that.

Apart from memory and cpu also additional limited resources like devices or hugepages influence how likely it is that a pod can go to the same node again.

**What you expected to happen**:

Instead of using a WFFC pod we should do the following:

 1) record on the VMI status that a DataVolume is used and if it is done with preparataions
 2) record on PVCs if annotations on it indicate that it is a DataVolume
 3) use this status info on the VMI status in virt-handler and virt-launcher to delay timeouts until the import opertions are done
 4) continue with the normal startup flow.

{"author": "person-5bccab16", "body": "Description:
*  There are three components of kubevirt with default installation: kubevirt-handler, kubevirt-controller, kubevirt-api, and kubevirt-operator, the kubevirt-handler is a daemon set running on each node, the controller&api&operator are deployments, each of them is two-pod deployments running on worker nodes randomly.
* There are different cluster roles of these components:
  *  The cluster role of the kubevirt-handler can patch nodes, which can be leveraged to make nodes unschedulable.
  * The cluster role of the kubevirt-controller can create pods/eviction, which can be leveraged to make pods evicted. While the cluster role of kubevirt-api can delete pods, which can be leveraged to make pods recreated and rescheduled to worker nodes.
  * The cluster role of the kubevirt-operator can list all secrets, which can be leveraged to get the admin secret of the entire cluster and make cluster-level privilege escalation.
* If a malicious user controls a worker node, which has kubevirt-handler, and one of kubevirt-api/controller:
  1.  He/she can leverage the kubevirt-handler to path all other nodes with unschedulable: true". And when the kubevirt-operator is rescheduled, the kubevirt-operator will be rescheduled to the malicious worker node.
  2. He/She can use the token of kubevirt-api/controller to evict/delete kubevirt-operator pods, which will be recreated and run on the malicious worker node.
  3. After the kubevirt-operator runs on the malicious worker node, he/she can leverage the operator's token to list all secrets in the whole cluster, get the cluster admin's token and make a cluster-level privilege escalation. 
* Mitigation Discussion:
  *  The cluster role of the kubevirt-operator can use the Resource Names to restrain the secrets which can be listed by the operator itself, however, it may need a careful review of the kubevirt-operator to identify all secrets needed by the operator exactly.
   *  The kubevirt-handler can remove the patch verbs of nodes, and the controller/api can remove the evict and delete of pods. However, similar to the first mitigation, it still needs a careful revisit of the components' source code.
   * The kubevirt can let the kubevirt-operator/controller/api runs on worker nodes (which we called "controller worker node") without running users' workloads, and leverage the isolation of nodes to mitigate the risk. However, if a malicious user leverages some method(i.e., scale-up of kubevirt-handler) and moves to the "controller worker node" horizontally, it still can break the worker nodes' isolation and make privilege escalation.
* Installation and environment:
   * We follow the Kubevirt's [official guide](https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/operations/installation/) to install the Kubevirt on a four-node Kubernetes cluster(1.24.2).
I'm looking forward to hearing back from you!

From my POV it is not specifically about k8s credential escalations. The thinking is about workload separation. See answer below.

> My point is: We can lock down virt-handler SA's permissions, and liimt them to a single node. But if we still allow a node to influence other workloads, then an actor on a node, can "simply" try to move workloads to it's own node, until there is a workload with sufficient privileges.
> 

> Thus to me the issue is two fold: Prevent that node can attract workloads, and prevent that workloads can be attracted to a node. It's two sides of the same medal.

Yes we are solving both. But on a different level than what I believe you are suggesting. Like mentioned above already: Attracting workloads is always possible, for instance via just registering your own device plugin and making a desired device available.

The core reason for differntiating between CP and Workers is not necessarily about k8s privileges. It is about separating more privileged components with more required access restrictions from workloads where more people can schedule things.

So: If I have a worker pool, the assumption already is that all the workloads in there have a common risk level. Eventually which node of those gets overtaken is a matter of luck, independent of device and hardware needs. Workloads will kind of randomly land on the compromised node or not. That is at least the mindset one has to have when looking at such a pool when doing risk and security assessments.

This leads then to the following: If I say that my app consists of workload A and workload B, A has more privileges than B, and B is more likely to be taken over (e.g. the public part of an app), I need to ensure that A and B will never scheduled on the same nodes (not even pod antiaffinity, is enough, since a node could have had B already there and be compromised now). You have to create sub-pools based on labels, similar like we do for CP and workloads in k8s.

Bottom line: If you think you can separate apps with different privileges  sufficiently based on some (maybe) existing hardware requirements, there is no sufficient separation in place, and that is not what we have to solve.

What we have to solve is:
 1. CP and worker pool separation can't be compromised by label updates
 2. Separations in any pools, created via labels by users or admins don't get compromised.

{"author": "person-e93fef33", "body": "<!-- Make sure that you visit our User Guide at https://kubevirt.io/user-guide.

**What happened**:

For a VM that is using "RerunOnFailure", if the virt-launcher pod get evicted (e.g. node drain), the VM will get shutdown but never come back online.
This also happens when explicitly delete the virt-launcher pod.


**What you expected to happen**:
tl;dr: The VM should stay running after Pod eviction.

From the doc: `A VirtualMachineInstance will be respawned if the previous instance failed in an error state. It will not be re-created if the guest stopped successfully (e.g. shut down from inside guest).`

IMO this feature is very useful to support "user explicitly want the VM guest to be down" comparing to "Always". However, we should get an exception for Pod eviction case which the guest stop is not initiated by user.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
1. Set VM runStrategy  as "RerunOnFailure"
2. Delete VM virt-launcher pod
3. Observe the VMI is in "Succeeded" phase under VMI.Status.Phase
4. Observe virt-launcher pod get never recreated

**Additional context**:

This issue doesn't seem to apply when using live migration as eviction strategy.

My understanding of what is happening after virt-launcher pod get evicted or deleted:

1. SIGTERM send inside to virt-launcher
2. Pod maybe get graceful or ungraceful shutdown.
3. VMI.Status.Phase will report to be "Succeeded": https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/cbe6f662786b5c5bfd872762019310d75c4fab19/pkg/virt-handler/vm.go#L3144
4. VMI controller will NOT recreate the virt-launcher pod: https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/9d68c4bdfcffb1d2d7015530ad2d341664d60364/pkg/virt-controller/watch/vmi.go#L1153
5. **What happened**:
When specifying a `kernelBoot.container.image` with an image which does not have a valid `initrd` or `kernel` (for example, an nginx container). The VMI is stuck terminating until the finalizer `foregroundDeleteVirtualMachine` is manually removed.

**What you expected to happen**:
Regardless of data provided in a VM manifest, the pod will be able to terminate and clean up after a period of time.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
Apply a VMI similar to this:
```yaml
apiVersion: kubevirt.io/v1
kind: VirtualMachineInstance
metadata:
  name: vmi-gets-stuck
spec:
  domain:
    cpu:
      model: host-passthrough
    devices:
      disks:
      - disk:
          bus: virtio
        name: containerdisk
      - disk:
          bus: virtio
        name: emptydisk
      interfaces:
      - bridge: {}
        name: default
    features:
      acpi:
        enabled: true
    firmware:
      bootloader:
        efi:
          secureBoot: false
      kernelBoot:
        container:
          image: nginx
          initrdPath: /sbin/init
    machine:
      type: q35
    resources:
      limits:
        cpu: "4"
        memory: 32Gi
  networks:
  - name: default
    pod: {}
  volumes:
  - containerDisk:
      image: tedezed/debian-container-disk:10.0
      imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
    name: containerdisk
  - emptyDisk:
      capacity: 64Gi
    name: emptydisk
```

	const kernelBootName = containerdisk.KernelBootName

	log.Log.Object(vmi).Infof("mounting kernel artifacts")

	if !util.HasKernelBootContainerImage(vmi) {
		log.Log.Object(vmi).Infof("kernel boot not defined - nothing to mount")
		return nil
	}

	kb := vmi.Spec.Domain.Firmware.KernelBoot.Container

	targetDir, err := containerdisk.GetDiskTargetDirFromHostView(vmi)
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("failed to get disk target dir: %v", err)
	}

	if err := safepath.MkdirAtNoFollow(targetDir, containerdisk.KernelBootName, 0755); err != nil {
		if !os.IsExist(err) {
			return err
		}
	}

	targetDir, err = safepath.JoinNoFollow(targetDir, containerdisk.KernelBootName)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if err := safepath.ChpermAtNoFollow(targetDir, 0, 0, 0755); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	socketFilePath, err := m.kernelBootSocketPathGetter(vmi)
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("failed to find socket path for kernel artifacts: %v", err)
	}


	record := vmiMountTargetRecord{
		MountTargetEntries: []vmiMountTargetEntry{{
			TargetFile: unsafepath.UnsafeAbsolute(targetDir.Raw()),

	err = m.addMountTargetRecord(vmi, &record)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	var targetInitrdPath *safepath.Path
	var targetKernelPath *safepath.Path

	if kb.InitrdPath != "" {
		if err := safepath.TouchAtNoFollow(targetDir, filepath.Base(kb.InitrdPath), 0655); err != nil && !os.IsExist(err) {
			return err
		}

		targetInitrdPath, err = safepath.JoinNoFollow(targetDir, filepath.Base(kb.InitrdPath))
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
	}

	if kb.KernelPath != "" {
		if err := safepath.TouchAtNoFollow(targetDir, filepath.Base(kb.KernelPath), 0655); err != nil && !os.IsExist(err) {
			return err
		}

		targetKernelPath, err = safepath.JoinNoFollow(targetDir, filepath.Base(kb.KernelPath))
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
	}

	areKernelArtifactsMounted := func(artifactsDir *safepath.Path, artifactFiles ...*safepath.Path) (bool, error) {
		if _, err = safepath.StatAtNoFollow(artifactsDir); errors.Is(err, os.ErrNotExist) {
			return false, nil
		} else if err != nil {
			return false, err
		}

		for _, mountPoint := range artifactFiles {
			if mountPoint != nil {
				isMounted, err := isolation.IsMounted(mountPoint)
				if !isMounted || err != nil {

	} else if !isMounted {

		kernelArtifacts, err := m.getKernelArtifactPaths(vmi)
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		if kernelArtifacts.kernel != nil {
			out, err := virt_chroot.MountChroot(kernelArtifacts.kernel, targetKernelPath, true).CombinedOutput()
			if err != nil {
				return fmt.Errorf("failed to bindmount %v: %v : %v", kernelBootName, string(out), err)
			}
		}

		if kernelArtifacts.initrd != nil {
			out, err := virt_chroot.MountChroot(kernelArtifacts.initrd, targetInitrdPath, true).CombinedOutput()
			if err != nil {
				return fmt.Errorf("failed to bindmount %v: %v : %v", kernelBootName, string(out), err)
			}
		}

	}

	if verify {
		mounted, err := areKernelArtifactsMounted(targetDir, targetInitrdPath, targetKernelPath)
		if err != nil {
			return fmt.Errorf("failed to check if kernel artifacts are mounted. error: %v", err)
		} else if !mounted {
			return fmt.Errorf("kernel artifacts verification failed")
		}
	}

	return nil

Address and size of the BAR
When you want to retrieve the actual base address of a BAR, be sure to mask the lower bits. For 16-bit Memory Space BARs, you calculate (BAR[x] & 0xFFF0). For 32-bit Memory Space BARs, you calculate (BAR[x] & 0xFFFFFFF0). For 64-bit Memory Space BARs, you calculate ((BAR[x] & 0xFFFFFFF0) + ((BAR[x + 1] & 0xFFFFFFFF) << 32)) For I/O Space BARs, you calculate (BAR[x] & 0xFFFFFFFC).

Before attempting to read the information about the BAR, make sure to disable both I/O and memory decode in the command byte. You can restore the original value after completing the BAR info read. This is needed as some devices are known to decode the write of all ones to the register as an (unintended) access.

To determine the amount of address space needed by a PCI device, you must save the original value of the BAR, write a value of all 1's to the register, then read it back. The amount of memory can then be determined by masking the information bits, performing a bitwise NOT ('~' in C), and incrementing the value by 1. The original value of the BAR should then be restored. The BAR register is naturally aligned and as such you can only modify the bits that are set. For example, if a device utilizes 16 MB it will have BAR0 filled with 0xFF000000 (0x1000000 after decoding) and you can only modify the upper 8-bits.   include <abstractions/passt>

  # Alternatively: include <abstractions/user-tmp>
  owner /tmp/**                         w,      # tap_sock_unix_init(), pcap(),
                                                # write_pidfile(),
                                                # logfile_init()

  owner @{HOME}/**                      w,      # pcap(), write_pidfile()
  mount,
  userns,

  network,
  capability,
  file,
  umount,
  # Host (privileged) processes may send signals to container processes.
  signal (receive) peer=unconfined,
  # runc may send signals to container processes.
  signal (receive) peer=runc,

  signal (receive) peer=crun,

**What happened**:
When we moved to Multus/`macvtap-cni` based networking our VMs as reported by `kubectl get vmi` started showing only IPv6 addresses. It works like that in ~90% of cases, sometimes correct IPv4 address is shown in `kubectl get vmi` and all IPv4 and IPv6 addresses are visible in `kubectl describe vmi`.

**What you expected to happen**:
The `ipAddress` in VMI status is primary IPv4 address of the VM and other addresses are included in `ipAddresses` in VMI status.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
Create VM with only `macvtap-cni` based networking.
Check IP reported by `kubectl get vmi`.

**Additional context**:
As we found out, since https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/pull/10799 the IP addresses detected by guest agent are ignored if there is any IP information available in virt-launcher pod. 
Monitoring VMI startup using `kubectl get vmi testvm -o jsonpath="{.status.interfaces}{'\n'}" -w` we got:
```

[{"infoSource":"multus-status","name":"hostnet"}]

[{"infoSource":"domain, guest-agent, multus-status","interfaceName":"eth0","mac":"8e:f5:20:f4:fa:df","name":"hostnet","queueCount":1}]
[{"infoSource":"domain, guest-agent, multus-status","interfaceName":"eth0","ipAddress":"10.244.55.240","ipAddresses":["10.244.55.240","fdfd:5c41:712d:d06f:8cf5:20ff:fef4:fadf","fe80::8cf5:20ff:fef4:fadf"],"mac":"8e:f5:20:f4:fa:df","name":"hostnet","queueCount":1}]
```
in the "good" few cases. Same VMI usually starts with following output:
```

**What happened**:
When cloning a VM which has a standalone volume (volume created by the user and not by DVTemplates) the restored cloned PVCs will remain without ownership.

**What you expected to happen**:
Expected that those PVC will be owned by the target VM.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
Create VMClone from a VM with standalone volume

**Additional context**:
The bug is happening since the Own process of the pvc (https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/pkg/storage/snapshot/restore.go#L971) is performed in a point in time where in case of Clone the target VM doesnt exist yet. It will be created later on in the restore process. 
In order to fix this need to move the ownership of the PVCs to after the target VM is updated/created.

Hey @person-2fba7b15! 👋 I'm here to help you out with any bugs or questions you have. Let's squash those bugs together!

<!-- Answer -->
I found a similar closed issue that might be relevant to your problem: [VM ownerReferences are not getting set on already existing disks(PVCs)](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/11519). The issue was resolved by updating to a newer version of KubeVirt where a fix was merged. Specifically, the fix ensures that the `virt-controller` will create the `DataVolume`, which should address the ownership problem once KubeVirt has version 1.2.1 and CDI has version 1.58.2 or 1.59.0.

In your case, the issue seems to be that the ownership assignment of the PVCs occurs before the target VM is created. To resolve this, you need to move the ownership assignment logic to a point in the process after the target VM has been created or updated. The specific conditions or checks performed in the `restore.go` file at line 971 related to PVC ownership are:

1. **Check if the `populatedForPVCAnnotation` is set correctly:**
   ```go
   if updatePVC.Annotations[populatedForPVCAnnotation] != dvName {
       if updatePVC.Annotations == nil {
           updatePVC.Annotations = make(map[string]string)
       }
       updatePVC.Annotations[populatedForPVCAnnotation] = dvName;
       // datavolume will take ownership
       updatePVC.OwnerReferences = nil;
       _, err = t.controller.Client.CoreV1().PersistentVolumeClaims(updatePVC.Namespace).Update(context.Background(), updatePVC, metav1.UpdateOptions{})
       if err != nil {
           return false, err;
       }
   }
   ```

2. **Set the `DataVolumeName` in the `VolumeRestore` status:**
   ```go
   vr.DataVolumeName = &dvName;
   updatedStatus = true;
   ```

These checks ensure that the PVC is correctly annotated for the DataVolume and that the DataVolume takes ownership of the PVC <sup>[[1]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/pkg/storage/snapshot/restore.go)</sup>.

To ensure that restored cloned PVCs get owned by the target VM, you need to specify the `PersistentVolumeClaim` in the `spec.volumes` section and reference it in the `spec.domain.devices.disks` section of the target VM's specification. Here is an example configuration:

```yaml
metadata:
  name: target-vm
apiVersion: kubevirt.io/v1
kind: VirtualMachineInstance
spec:
  domain:
    resources:
      requests:
        memory: 64M
    devices:
      disks:
      - name: clonedpvcdisk
        disk: {}
  volumes:
    - name: clonedpvcdisk
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: cloned-pvc
```

This ensures that the cloned PVC is correctly associated with the target VM <sup>[[2]](https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/storage/disks_and_volumes)</sup>.

The files, including `virtio-win-gt-x64.msi`, are visible in the container disk image on Linux but not showing up in Windows because the virtio drivers are distributed in a form of a container disk that needs to be attached to the VirtualMachine as a CD-ROM. If the container disk is not properly attached or recognized by the Windows VM, the files will not be visible.

To ensure the virtio drivers are available in Windows, you need to attach the virtio-win package as a SATA CD-ROM to the VirtualMachine. Here is how you can do it:

```yaml
spec:
  domain:
    devices:
      disks:
        - name: virtiocontainerdisk
          cdrom:
            bus: sata
volumes:
  - containerDisk:
      image: quay.io/kubevirt/virtio-container-disk
    name: virtiocontainerdisk
```

Make sure the virtio container disk is properly attached and recognized by the Windows VM. Once attached, you should be able to see and access the files, including `virtio-win-gt-x64.msi`, in Windows <sup>[[1]](https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/user_workloads/windows_virtio_drivers)</sup>.

{"author": "person-0ae064df", "body": "**What happened**:
Custom authorized SSH keys that were added to the file `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` are removed by kubevirt.

**What you expected to happen**:
The custom keys should not be removed.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
1. Create a secret with a public SSH key.
2. Create a VM with `AccessCredentials` that refer the secret and use the `qemuGuestAgent` propagation method.
3. Run the VM, log in and add a second key to `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`.
4. Change the key in the secret, and wait until it is propagated to the VM.

The `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` will not contain the second key that was not added by kubevirt.

", "closed_by": null, "comments": [{"author": "person-0ae064df", "body": "/cc @person-0ae064df ", "body_missing": false, "created_at": "2024-10-17T14:41:58Z", "id": 2419745907}, {"author": "person-43cbd26d", "body": "<!-- Greeting -->
Hey @person-0ae064df, I'm here to help you with this issue. I can assist with bug fixes, answer questions, and guide you on how to contribute. Let's tackle this together!

<!-- Answer -->
Custom authorized SSH keys in the `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` file are removed by KubeVirt when using the `qemuGuestAgent` propagation method because the file is managed by the guest agent. Any changes to the file not made through the guest agent will be overwritten. To prevent this, ensure that any SSH key modifications are made through the guest agent by updating the attached Kubernetes `Secret`. This way, the changes will be applied to the running virtual machine immediately. Additionally, you can specify the users who should have the SSH public keys added to their `authorized_keys` file by configuring the `users` property in the `qemuGuestAgent` configuration, ensuring that the keys are correctly propagated to the intended users <sup>[[1]](https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/user_workloads/accessing_virtual_machines)</sup><sup>[[2]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/pkg/virt-operator/resource/generate/components/validations_generated.go)</sup>.

{"author": "person-1118c074", "body": "**What happened**:

Consider a pre-copy  Virtual Machine Instance Migration.
The migration has been successfully completed. The domain is successfully running in the target pod.
However, the source pod crashed before it could update the domain metadata or the virt-handler on the node. 
As a result, virt-handler can't finalize the migration and update the VMIM object. 
Since the source pod failed, VMI object is failed as well. 
Consequently, the target virt-handler deletes the running target pod, since the VMI is in a Final state, even though the migration had actually succeeded.


**What you expected to happen**:
I expected the migration to be identified as successful, with KubeVirt recognizing that the target pod was running. The system should have updated the VMIM and VMI objects appropriately, ensuring the VMI would continue to operate.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

Specifically, the file `pkg/virt-operator/resource/generate/components/crds.go` contains functions that generate all necessary CRDs for KubeVirt, such as `VirtualMachineInstance`, `VirtualMachine`, `VirtualMachineInstanceReplicaSet`, and others <sup>[[1]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/pkg/virt-operator/resource/generate/components/crds.go)</sup>.

To manually install these CRDs, you can extract them from the KubeVirt release manifests or directly from the repository and apply them using `kubectl`. Here's a general approach:

1. **Download the CRD Definitions**: You can download the CRD YAML files from the KubeVirt GitHub releases page corresponding to your version (v1.3.1 in your case).

2. **Apply the CRDs**: Use `kubectl` to apply the CRD YAML files to your cluster:
   ```bash
   kubectl apply -f <path-to-crd-yaml>
   ```

Regarding why they might not be part of the official installation docs, it's possible that the installation process assumes these CRDs are included in the operator manifest or that they are automatically managed by the operator. {"author": "person-a2c0ed82", "body": "**What happened**:
We use the following code in order to advertise virtlogd log entries:
https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/87475917dfaa4ce325c4cff88075ecca16ea23ff/pkg/virt-launcher/virtwrap/util/libvirt_helper.go#L301-L313

The following loop iterates on the log file, then immediately breaks when done reading it, instead of waiting for more log entries:
```go
 for scanner.Scan() { 
 	log.LogQemuLogLine(log.Log, scanner.Text()) 
 } 
```

In order to test this, I've created a tiny POC [1], which results in the loop breaking almost immediately:

{"component":"virt-launcher","level":"error","msg":"virtlogd: scanner EXITED!","pos":"libvirt_helper.go:320","timestamp":"2024-12-02T08:32:24.985723Z"}
```

The relevant goroutine should wait for more log entries to come and not break immediately.

100% reproducible. You can follow the [POC](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/compare/main...person-a2c0ed82:kubevirt:POC/virtlogd-logging-bug) and gather the logs as I've shown above.

- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`): v1.29.11

", "closed_by": null, "comments": [{"author": "person-43cbd26d", "body": "<!-- Answer -->
The issue you're encountering is that the `scanner.Scan()` loop in the `libvirt_helper.go` file stops immediately after reading the current contents of the log file, instead of waiting for new log entries. This behavior is due to the `bufio.NewScanner` not inherently supporting continuous reading of a file that is being appended to, such as a log file.

To address this, you can implement a mechanism to continuously watch the file for new entries. One approach is to use a file-watching library that supports tailing, such as the `nxadm/tail` package, which is already used in the KubeVirt codebase for similar purposes. This package can handle log rotation and continuously stream new log entries as they are written to the file.

Here's a basic outline of how you might modify the code to use `nxadm/tail`:

1. Replace the `bufio.NewScanner` with `nxadm/tail.TailFile` to start tailing the log file.
2. Use the `Tail.Lines` channel to process new log lines as they are added to the file.

This approach will allow the log reading loop to wait for new entries and process them as they arrive, addressing the issue of the loop exiting prematurely.

<!-- Answer -->
Your understanding is correct. When you call `removeVolume` on a hotplugged volume using `virtctl`, the volume is removed from the VMI spec but remains in the status. The `virt-controller` then proceeds to remove the attachment pod without waiting for the volume to be fully detached from the QEMU process via libvirt. {"author": "person-8a180528", "body": "**What happened**:
Have a multus network using whereabouts. Things seemed to be working well, until I live migrated a vm, then launched a new vm.

Before launching the new vm, I could see the migrated vm on the network. It had the expected ip.

On launching the new vm, it also got assigned the migrated vm's ip.

Doing a describe on the migrated vm's vmi showed it having a different whereabouts ip. same in the whereabouts ip.

So, during migration it seems the ip is preserved in the vm properly, but the new pod gets a new ip assigned to it and the old one is dropped, allowing it to be reassigned.

**What you expected to happen**:
Migration would still reserve the ip so other vms wont pick it up.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
Configure a network via whereabouts. launch a vm, migrate it, then add another vm. both will have the same ip

**Environment**:
- KubeVirt version (use `virtctl version`): v1.3.0

", "closed_by": null, "comments": [{"author": "person-43cbd26d", "body": "<!-- Answer -->
I found a similar closed issue regarding IP address handling during VM migrations with Whereabouts, but no solution was found in the comments. You can view the issue [here](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/10579) <sup>[[1]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/10579)</sup>. 

In your case, it seems that during the migration, the IP is not being reserved properly, leading to reassignment. This might be related to how the Whereabouts CNI plugin manages IP address reservations and releases. The plugin uses Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) for IP pools and overlapping range IP reservations, which might need to be configured to ensure IP persistence across migrations <sup>[[2]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirtci/blob/main/cluster-provision/k8s/1.31/manifests/whereabouts/whereabouts-v0.6.1.yaml)</sup><sup>[[3]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirtci/blob/main/cluster-provision/k8s/1.32/manifests/whereabouts/whereabouts-v0.6.1.yaml)</sup><sup>[[4]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirtci/blob/main/cluster-provision/gocli/opts/cnao/manifests/whereabouts.yaml)</sup>. 

You might want to check the configuration of the Whereabouts plugin to ensure that IP addresses are reserved correctly during migrations.

**What happened**:
After the commit in QEMU (https://github.com/qemu/qemu/commit/75997e182b695f2e3f0a2d649734952af5caf3ee), QEMU no longer truncates the serial number for disks connected via SCSI and instead returns an error if the serial exceeds 36 characters.

**What you expected to happen**:
The VM creation should fail due to validation rules preventing the use of serial numbers longer than 36 characters.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
1. Create a VM with a disk connected via SCSI.
2. Set a serial number longer than 36 characters.
3. Observe the error during VM creation.

**Additional context**:
**Error message example:**
```

      The serial number can''t be longer than 36 characters'')"'
    reason: Synchronizing with the Domain failed.
    status: "False"
    type: Synchronized
```

The issue you're encountering is due to a recent change in QEMU's handling of SCSI disk serial numbers. QEMU now enforces a strict limit of 36 characters for serial numbers, and any attempt to use a longer serial number results in an error during VM creation.

To address this, you should ensure that the serial numbers for SCSI disks in your VM specifications do not exceed 36 characters. This can be done by validating the serial number length before VM creation. If you're using KubeVirt, you might need to implement or adjust validation logic to enforce this limit, ensuring that any serial number provided is within the allowed length.

VM with improper firmware UUID cannot be properly stopped. 
Its corresponding VMI is stuck in `Scheduled` phase.  User needs to wait for some period of time until the cleanup
happens and the VMI object disappears.

**What you expected to happen**:

4. `virtctl start vm-cirros`
5. Wait until VMI phase is `Scheduled`
6. Observe VMI status via `kubectl describe vmi vm-cirros`
7. Locate the libvirt error `server error. command SyncVMI failed: "LibvirtError(Code=35, Domain=20, Message='malformed <sysinfo> uuid element')"`

", "closed_by": null, "comments": [{"author": "person-7f4cdc94", "body": "/sig compute", "body_missing": false, "created_at": "2025-02-15T14:37:33Z", "id": 2660951048}, {"author": "person-43cbd26d", "body": "<!-- Greeting -->
Hey there, @person-7f4cdc94! I'm a bot designed to help you with bugs, questions, and becoming a contributor. Feel free to ask for assistance while waiting for a human maintainer.

<!-- Answer -->
In KubeVirt, when a Virtual Machine Instance (VMI) encounters an error due to a malformed UUID in its domain specification, it can result in the VMI being stuck in the `Scheduled` phase. This is because the malformed UUID causes a libvirt error, preventing the VMI from transitioning to a `Succeeded` or `Failed` state immediately.

To address this issue, you can manually delete the VMI using `kubectl delete vmi <vmi-name>`. This action should trigger the cleanup process, moving the VMI to a `Failed` state if the `virt-handler` is responsive. If the node or `virt-handler` is unresponsive, you may need to force-delete the associated pod using `kubectl delete pod --force --grace-period=0 <pod-name>`. This will help expedite the cleanup process and allow you to correct the UUID and restart the VM without waiting for the automatic timeout <sup>[[1]](https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/cluster_admin/unresponsive_nodes)</sup>.

For a more permanent solution, consider implementing validation checks during the VMI creation process to catch malformed UUIDs and prevent such errors from occurring.

{"author": "person-7f4cdc94", "body": "**What happened**:
VM restore object failed to complete because the target VM is already exists. However when I delete the target VM
The restore doesn't happen and suddenly the VM restore object itself also disappears.

**What you expected to happen**:
VM restore controller to eventually restore the VM, since target VM was deleted and restore can proceed.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
1. Create Cirros VM from project examples `examples/vm-cirros.yaml` (no need to launch the VM)
2. Create VM snapshot, source is the Cirros VM
```
kind: VirtualMachineSnapshot
metadata:
  name: snapshot-vm-cirros
spec:
  source:
    apiGroup: kubevirt.io
    kind: VirtualMachine
    name: vm-cirros
```
3. Wait for snapshot to complete.
4. Create VM restore object for `vm-cirros`
```
kind: VirtualMachineRestore
metadata:
  name: vm-restore-cirros
spec:
  target:
    apiGroup: kubevirt.io
    kind: VirtualMachine
    name: vm-cirros
  virtualMachineSnapshotName: snapshot-vm-cirros
```
5. Observe the VM restore status, should error with target already exists
6. Delete the vm-cirros VM
7. Observe the VM restore, it should disappear as well.

**Additional context**:
Add any other context about the problem here.

**Environment**:
- KubeVirt version (use `virtctl version`): main", "closed_by": null, "comments": [{"author": "person-7f4cdc94", "body": "/sig compute", "body_missing": false, "created_at": "2025-02-15T14:37:15Z", "id": 2660950953}, {"author": "person-43cbd26d", "body": "<!-- Answer -->
The VM restore object disappears after deleting the target VM because the restore process is tightly coupled with the existence of the target VM. When the target VM is deleted, the restore process cannot proceed as it relies on the target VM to apply the restore operations. The `vmRestoreTarget` struct in the code is responsible for managing the restore process, and it includes methods that check for the existence of the target VM. If the target VM does not exist, the restore process cannot be completed, leading to the disappearance of the VM restore object <sup>[[1]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/pkg/storage/snapshot/restore.go)</sup>.

Currently, there is no mechanism to automatically retry the restore process if the target VM is deleted and then recreated. The restore operation is not allowed if the target VM already exists and is different from the source VM, which is why you encountered an error initially <sup>[[2]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/pkg/storage/admitters/vmrestore_test.go)</sup>.

3. **Feature Gates**: You mentioned enabling the `Root` feature gate. Ensure that this configuration is correctly applied and that it aligns with your environment's requirements.

4. **Emulation Mode**: Since you are using a Kind cluster on MacOS, ensure that the emulation mode is correctly set, as you did with the `useEmulation` patch. This is crucial for environments that do not support hardware virtualization.

5. **Check Compatibility**: Verify that the KubeVirt version you are using is compatible with your Kubernetes version and the Kind cluster setup.

If these steps do not resolve the issue, consider checking the KubeVirt and Kind documentation for any additional configuration requirements specific to your environment.

This introduced some errors that are timing-dependant after the migration (see [0]), `TimeDefinedCache` doesn't take into account the possibility to receive an empty `DomainStats`, because querying libvirt "too early", caching a `nil`result in consequence:
"""
After migrating, `KeepValueUpdated()` queries the `DomainStats` before libvirt can respond, so libvirt returns them empty. The `TimeDefinedCache` does not consider this case and cached a nil. Since `lastRefresh` has been updated, the following queries return the cached value (i.e., `nil`), causing some migration tests and the scrapper to fail sometimes. 
"""

It's not clear to me that this cache is really required, since from the commit messages it seems the `DomainStats` are checked periodically. 
But, in any case, this functionality should be part of libvirt, since it "knows" when that information should be invalidated. I just did a quick fix in [0], as part of moving the `donwardMetrics` virtio-serial server from the handler to the launcher. Hey @person-3098ddbc! I'm here to help you with any bugs, questions, or to guide you on your journey to becoming a contributor. Let's tackle this together!

<!-- Answer -->
To address the issue with PCI passthrough of consumer GPUs like the RTX 3090 or RTX 4090, where both audio and video devices are involved, you can follow these steps:

1. **Set `externalResourceProvider: false`:** In the KubeVirt Custom Resource (CR) configuration, set `externalResourceProvider: false`. This helps manage the environment variables set by the kubevirt-gpu-device-plugin for all GPU devices in the same IOMMU group.

2. **Enable IOMMU and Virtualization Extensions:** Ensure that the IOMMU extension (Intel VT-d or AMD IOMMU) and virtualization extensions are enabled in the BIOS. For Intel CPUs, add `intel_iommu=on` to the kernel parameters, and for AMD CPUs, add `amd_iommu=on`.

3. **Use the vfio-pci Driver:** Ensure that the vfio-pci driver is used for GPU passthrough. Load the vfio-pci kernel module on the host using:
   ```
   # modprobe vfio-pci
   ```

4. **Bind the GPU to the vfio-pci Driver:** Unbind the GPU from its original driver and bind it to the vfio-pci driver. Identify the PCI address of the GPU using:
   ```
   $ lspci -DD | grep NVIDIA
   ```
   Then, bind the device to the vfio-pci driver:
   ```
   echo 0000:01:00.0 > /sys/bus/pci/drivers/nvidia/unbind
   echo "vfio-pci" > /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000\:01\:00.0/driver_override
   echo 0000:01:00.0 > /sys/bus/pci/drivers/vfio-pci/bind
   ```

5. **Allowlist Permitted Devices:** Ensure that the GPU is allowlisted in the KubeVirt CR by its `vendor:product` selector. For example:
   ```yaml
   configuration:
     permittedHostDevices:
       pciHostDevices:
       - pciVendorSelector: "10DE:2204"
         resourceName: "nvidia.com/GA102_GeForce_RTX_3090"
   ```

These steps should help resolve the PCI passthrough issues for consumer GPUs in a KubeVirt environment <sup>[[1]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/13925)</sup><sup>[[2]](https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/compute/host-devices)</sup>.

This is because the video and audio components of a GPU are often part of the same IOMMU group, and they need to be handled together to ensure proper functionality.

   ```bash

   echo 0000:01:00.0 > /sys/bus/pci/drivers/vfio-pci/bind

   echo 0000:01:00.1 > /sys/bus/pci/drivers/snd_hda_intel/unbind
   echo "vfio-pci" > /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000\:01\:00.1/driver_override
   echo 0000:01:00.1 > /sys/bus/pci/drivers/vfio-pci/bind
   ```

2. **Ensure Proper Configuration:** In your KubeVirt configuration, ensure that both components are included in the `permittedHostDevices` section, similar to how the video component is configured.

By ensuring both components are properly configured and passed through, you should be able to avoid issues with GPU passthrough in your production environment.

**What happened**:
Link : https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/network/hotplug_interfaces/#removing-an-interface-from-a-running-vm

We observe a stale veth interface (example: 9a6a0c3b4d8-nic@if73) left  in the virt-launcher pod and on the worker node after hot-unplug operation

Please note that this interface was added during the hotplug operation but was not removed during the hot-unplug operation.

Additionally, this issue occurs only with in-place hot-unplugged interfaces; we do not encounter this issue with migration-based hot-unplugs.


More details at: https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/13721#issuecomment-2679321713

**What you expected to happen**:
Hot-unplug should remove/clean up interfaces that were added during the hotplug operation.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
1) create VM with below yaml
```
apiVersion: kubevirt.io/v1
kind: VirtualMachine
metadata:
  name: vm-fedora-ap
  annotations:
    kubevirt.io/libvirt-log-filters: "2:qemu.qemu_monitor 3:*"  
spec:
  runStrategy: Always
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        kubevirt.io/domain: vm-fedora-ap
        special: key  
    spec:
      domain:
        devices:
          disks:
          - disk:
              bus: virtio
            name: containerdisk
          interfaces:
          - name: default
            masquerade: {}
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: 1Gi
      networks:
      - name: default
        pod: {}
      volumes:
      - containerDisk:
          image: quay.io/kubevirt/fedora-with-test-tooling-container-disk:20250203_61a94ee17a-s390x
        name: containerdisk
```

The issue you're experiencing with stale interfaces after an in-place hot-unplug operation in KubeVirt is a known problem. This occurs when the interface added during the hotplug operation is not properly removed during the hot-unplug operation, leaving behind a stale virtual Ethernet (veth) interface in the virt-launcher pod and on the worker node. This issue is specific to in-place hot-unplug operations and does not occur with migration-based hot-unplugs.

The expected behavior is for the hot-unplug operation to clean up any interfaces that were added during the hotplug operation. The logs you provided from the multus and multus-dynamic network controller pods indicate that the removal process was initiated, but the interface was not fully cleaned up.

This issue has been discussed in the KubeVirt community, and there are ongoing efforts to address it. You mentioned that the GitHub issue #13721 might be resolved by pull request #13848, with additional references to pull requests #13941 and #14025. These pull requests may contain fixes or improvements related to the hot-unplug process.

1. **`mknod` Command Error**: The error indicates a missing operand in the `mknod` command. The correct syntax for creating a KVM device node should be:
   ```sh
   mknod /dev/kvm c 10 $(grep '\<kvm\>' /proc/misc | cut -f 1 -d' ')
   ```

2. **Container Not Running**: This could be due to several reasons, such as missing environment variables or container runtime issues. Also, verify that your container runtime (Docker or Podman) is correctly configured and running <sup>[[2]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/kubevirtci/cluster-up/cluster/ephemeral-provider-common.sh)</sup>.

For the Bazel build error:

1. **Timeout and Container Registry Issues**: Ensure that your network connection is stable and that you have access to the required container registries. You might need to configure proxy settings if you're behind a firewall.

2. **Visibility Issues**: The `BUILD.bazel` file should have the correct visibility settings. {"author": "person-491add6c", "body": "**What happened**:
I set the `kubectl.kubernetes.io/default-container` annotation on my VMI to `guest-console-log`:
```
apiVersion: kubevirt.io/v1
kind: VirtualMachineInstance
metadata:
  annotations:
    kubectl.kubernetes.io/default-container: guest-console-log
```

However the virt-launcher-pod is still set to `compute`:
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  annotations:
    kubectl.kubernetes.io/default-container: compute
```

**What you expected to happen**:
I expected the virt-launcher pod to inherit the annotation. I am setting other annotations on the VMI that the virt-launcher pod is properly inheriting.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
1. Add `kubectl.kubernetes.io/default-container` annotation to the VMI spec, e.g:

```
Spec: kubevirtcorev1.VirtualMachineSpec{
	Running: ptr.To(true),
	Template: &kubevirtcorev1.VirtualMachineInstanceTemplateSpec{
		ObjectMeta: k8smetav1.ObjectMeta{
			Name:        resource.Name,
			Labels:      labels,
			Annotations: annotations, // INCLUDE HERE
		},
		...
	},
},
```
2. Create VMI
3. Observe that virt-launcher pod does not inherit it.

**Environment**:
- KubeVirt version (use `virtctl version`): v1.1.1
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`): v1.28.2
- VM or VMI specifications: N/A
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration: N/A
- OS (e.g. from /etc/os-release): `22.04.5 LTS (Jammy Jellyfish)`

<!-- Answer -->
The `virt-launcher` pod does not inherit the `kubectl.kubernetes.io/default-container` annotation from the VirtualMachineInstance (VMI) because the `filterVMIAnnotationsForPod` function in KubeVirt explicitly filters out annotations with the prefix `kubectl.kubernetes.io`. This function is responsible for determining which annotations from the VMI should be copied to the pod, and it excludes any annotations with the `kubectl.kubernetes.io` prefix, including `kubectl.kubernetes.io/default-container` <sup>[[1]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/pkg/virt-controller/services/template.go)</sup>.

The issue you're experiencing, where the virt-launcher pod goes from Ready 3/3 to Error 2/3 after adding a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC), is likely due to the PVC not existing in the namespace where you're deploying your VirtualMachine. Ensure that the PVC named `vivado-volume` is created and available in the same namespace as your VirtualMachine. If the PVC does not exist, the pod will fail to attach the volume, resulting in the error state you're seeing <sup>[[1]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/565a1cab6ccd28d54c6bc0834a4ba120bef68bd8/pkg/virt-controller/services/template_test.go#L2484-L2530)</sup>.

Should the filesystem size on the node be a relevant factor when attaching a PVC?", "body_missing": false, "created_at": "2025-03-14T06:47:26Z", "id": 2723800529}, {"author": "person-43cbd26d", "body": "<!-- Answer -->
Yes, the filesystem size on the node is a relevant factor when attaching a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) in KubeVirt. The error message indicates that the available space on the node's filesystem is less than the requested size for the `vivado-volume` disk image. KubeVirt checks the available space and compares it to the requested size. If the available space is less than the requested size, it may attempt to shrink the requested size within a tolerable limit, but if the space is still insufficient, it will result in an error <sup>[[1]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/pkg/host-disk/host-disk.go)</sup>.

I have a 1TB PVC and nodes can't host 1TB locally.", "body_missing": false, "created_at": "2025-03-14T06:54:17Z", "id": 2723808729}, {"author": "person-43cbd26d", "body": "<!-- Answer -->
To handle cases where a large 1TB PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) is needed in KubeVirt, but the nodes cannot host 1TB locally, you can use a StorageClass with `volumeBindingMode` set to `WaitForFirstConsumer`. This approach delays the binding and provisioning of the PersistentVolume (PV) until a Pod using the PVC is created. KubeVirt can schedule a special ephemeral pod that acts as the first consumer of the PVC. This pod is scheduled to a node capable of running the VM, triggering Kubernetes to provision and bind the PV on the same node. Once the PVCs are bound, the Containerized Data Importer (CDI) can perform its tasks, and KubeVirt can start the actual VM.

Additionally, KubeVirt provides a mechanism to replace PVCs with HostDisks when the PVC is not in BlockMode. This allows the filesystem PersistentVolumeClaim to be mounted into the pod as a directory from the node filesystem, which can help manage storage constraints by using the node's local storage more flexibly <sup>[[1]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/docs/localstorage-disks.md)</sup><sup>[[2]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/pkg/host-disk/host-disk.go)</sup>.

", "body_missing": false, "created_at": "2025-03-14T06:55:21Z", "id": 2723809838}, {"author": "person-f08405b0", "body": "So is there a mechanism to attach a (shared) PVC from a storage node that doesn't fit on the host node to a KubeVirt VM?", "body_missing": false, "created_at": "2025-03-14T22:14:45Z", "id": 2725892703}, {"author": "person-43cbd26d", "body": "<!-- Answer -->
Yes, there is a mechanism to attach a shared PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) from a storage node that doesn't fit on the host node to a KubeVirt Virtual Machine (VM). You can use a StorageClass with `volumeBindingMode` set to `WaitForFirstConsumer`. This delays the binding and provisioning of the PersistentVolume (PV) until a Pod using the PVC is created. KubeVirt can schedule a special ephemeral pod that acts as the first consumer of the PVC, ensuring it is scheduled to a node capable of running the VM. This triggers Kubernetes to provision and bind the PV on the same node, allowing the VM to start once the PVCs are bound.

Additionally, KubeVirt supports hotplugging volumes, which allows you to dynamically attach and detach volumes to a running VM. This feature can be particularly useful for managing storage resources that need to be shared or moved between nodes without stopping the VM <sup>[[1]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/docs/localstorage-disks.md)</sup><sup>[[2]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/pkg/virt-controller/watch/vmi/volume-hotplug.go)</sup>.

**What happened**:
Hi all,
I am trying to boot a Fedora 41 Cloud image with a self compiled kernel image and initramfs. When doing this I am getting stuck while booting the kernel.

**What you expected to happen**:
Successfully booting the kernel.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
For this I am using the following user guide:
https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/user_workloads/boot_from_external_source/#workflow

1. Extract the kernel image and initramfs from the cloud image:
```

  -smp 8 \
  -nographic \
  -device virtio-net-pci,netdev=net0 \

FROM scratch

docker push container-registry.local:5000/custom-fedora-cloudcontainer:6.11.4

EOF


kubectl apply -f boot-kernel.yaml

virtctl console boot-kernel

I found a similar closed issue where users experienced network loss after a VM restart. The suggested solutions include:

1. Reading the IP from the VMI status and using it for SSH connections.
2. Using a Kubernetes Service to track the VM's IP.
3. Using a secondary interface network and defining its IP using cloud-init.
4. Using a third-party or a D/S project/product that provides sticky IPs to pods/VMs.

Additionally, you might want to explore using the IPAM extensions available at [kubevirt/ipam-extensions](https://github.com/kubevirt/ipam-extensions), although it may involve dealing with several moving parts <sup>[[1]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/12266)</sup>.

Another related issue was resolved by addressing a problem with randomly generated MAC addresses on VM startup. To ensure a consistent MAC address, you can explicitly define it in the VM Spec or use KubeMacPool to automate the MAC address assignment <sup>[[2]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/9993)</sup>.

These solutions might help resolve the network loss issue you're experiencing after restarting the VM.

A similar issue was reported in a closed thread, where a "permission denied" error occurred while opening a PVC device <sup>[[1]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/11002)</sup>. Unfortunately, no solution was found in the comments of that issue.

To troubleshoot the "permission denied" error you're encountering, you can follow these steps:

1. **Check Ownership of Block Devices**: Ensure that the block devices have the correct ownership. The function `changeOwnershipOfBlockDevices` in KubeVirt is responsible for changing the ownership of block devices associated with a Virtual Machine Instance (VMI). Verify that this function is executed correctly and that the `OwnershipManager` is configured to use the appropriate user and group for ownership settings <sup>[[2]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/pkg/virt-handler/non-root.go)</sup><sup>[[3]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/pkg/ephemeral-disk-utils/utils.go)</sup>.

2. **Security Contexts**: Review the security contexts of the pods involved in the data import process. Ensure that they have the necessary permissions to access block devices.

3. **Storage Class Configuration**: Double-check the storage class configuration, especially the `rook-ceph-block` storage class, to ensure it is set up correctly and supports the required access modes and volume binding modes.

By following these steps, you should be able to identify and resolve the permission issues with accessing the block device.

**What happened**:
In PR #12848 the CompletionTimeoutPerGiB parameter was reduced from 800s to 150s. This makes sense for live migrations, but at the moment the volume migration feature also uses this parameter. As a result, volume migrations keep getting cancelled and retried forever if the storage copy does not progress fast enough. Raising the CompletionTimeoutPerGiB parameter back to 800s fixes this, but obviously brings back the pitfalls for live migrations.

**What you expected to happen**:
The CompletionTimeoutPerGiB parameter should not apply to storage migrations. Since this is already an expensive operation, it makes little sense to ever cancel and retry storage migrations to begin with, except for maybe when no progress has been made at all for several minutes.

Please implement a new optional parameter to set a progress timeout for specifically storage migrations, and ignore the CompletionTimeoutPerGiB parameter for storage migrations.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
1. Set CompletionTimeoutPerGiB to 150s
2. Create a VM with 80GB of data
3. Trigger a storage migration and follow the virt-launcher pod logs
4. Notice the storage migration gets canceled and retried over and over.
5. Cancel the storage migration and increase the CompletionTimeoutPerGiB to 800s
6. Retry the storage migration and notice it completes successfully

With these configs, the timeout would be `150*80 == 12000 seconds == 3.3 hours`, which means you'd need a bandwidth of `80,000 MB / 12000 seconds ≈ 6.67 MB/s` to complete this in time. Is it something we think most environments would handle?

For compute migration we know there are alternative techniques to switch to and cases where a migration technique should be abandoned due to progress not being fast enough to handle new dirty pages. So the idea of taking the entire memory content, multiplying that by some per-GB value and that result becoming the total timeout we test for, makes sense there.

In the case of a storage migration I'm not sure if this approach works. Essentially we have to separate the storage to copy in 2 sections: all existing storage and new storage transactions since the migration started. For all existing storage, we shouldn't care how long it takes to copy, as long as it keeps making progress. So only when 0 bytes have been copied since the last X seconds, should we assume something went wrong and restart the migration. Once this part has fully completed, all that's left is the storage transactions since the migration started. Here you come back to the same strategy as compute migrations, where all we really want is a faster migration pace than the storage dirty transactions pace. But even then, since the storage operation is so expensive, it's better to keep trying to catch up than to abandon the whole storage copy and restart from scratch. The copy could be for TBs of VM disks and we really shouldn't try to copy this more than once.

So I would recommend for a timeout that purely tests for how long 0 bytes of progress was made. Let the user abandon the storage migration manually if the rate of dirty I/O is too high, or manually stop the app to reduce the dirty I/O pace.


The goal of the timeout should be to catch dead migrations where progress has halted. KubeVirt currently does not provide a way to specify PCI devices using XML like virsh, nor does it allow users to select specific PCI bus addresses during passthrough. {"author": "person-b644da65", "body": "**Description:**
Guestless VMIs are created via the following function in the KubeVirt codebase:
https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/47ac60cbb588b7721b47e200b952b7145bf573c9/tests/libvmifact/factory.go#L100

The NewGuestless() function is intended to spin up a minimal virtual machine with no disk or OS, primarily for testing purposes. This works as expected on x86_64 platforms, as QEMU can launch VMs even without a disk or boot image.

However, this approach fails on s390x. The s390x architecture requires an Initial Program Load (IPL) to boot any virtual machine—even for minimal test scenarios.

**Documentation:**
https://www.qemu.org/docs/master/system/s390x/bootdevices.html

**Observed Behavior:**
Attempting to create a guestless VM on s390x results in the following QEMU error:

```
[root@ ~]# /usr/libexec/qemu-kvm  -machine s390-ccw-virtio -display none -nographic -d int
LOADPARM=[        ]
Could not find a suitable boot device (none specified)
Failed to load OS from hard disk
```
The above error/panic is thrown from QEMU code at:

https://gitlab.com/qemu-project/qemu/-/blob/v8.2.0/pc-bios/s390-ccw/main.c#L290

https://gitlab.com/qemu-project/qemu/-/blob/v8.2.0/pc-bios/s390-ccw/main.c#L305

Using -no-shutdown prevents QEMU from exiting immediately, but the error remains and the VM does not boot.

Root Cause:

The s390x platform requires a valid bootloader and an IPL source in order to start any VM. Without a defined disk or boot device, the IPL process cannot begin. This differs from x86_64 behavior, where a VM can be launched without a boot image. 

Since NewGuestless() does not attach a disk, kernel, or initrd, the resulting VM cannot successfully perform IPL on s390x.

From QEMU docs:

"For classical mainframe guests (i.e. LPAR or z/VM installations), you always have to explicitly specify the disk where you want to boot from (or 'IPL' from, in s390x-speak – IPL means 'Initial Program Load')."

**Proposed Workaround:**

As guestless VMIs are incompatible with s390x, we suggest using Alpine-based VMIs (or any minimal VMI with a valid disk and boot path) instead of the NewGuestless() implementation when running tests on s390x.
We need this to enable sig-compute lane for s390x
for example at : https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/28cb4bf47bd457a6b86ad8b47d883b66c8322cd1/tests/compute/vm_lifecycle.go#L213", "closed_by": null, "comments": [{"author": "person-43cbd26d", "body": "<!-- Answer -->
The `NewGuestless()` function in the KubeVirt codebase creates minimal virtual machines without disks or operating systems, which works on x86_64 architectures but fails on s390x due to its requirement for an Initial Program Load (IPL) from a valid boot device. The s390x architecture mandates a specified disk or boot device to initiate the IPL process, which is not provided by `NewGuestless()`, leading to a QEMU error indicating no suitable boot device was found.

To address this issue on s390x, it is recommended to use Alpine-based VMIs or any minimal VMI that includes a valid disk and boot path instead of relying on `NewGuestless()`. This adjustment is necessary to enable the sig-compute lane for s390x.

The issue you're encountering with the Passt binding plugin during the migration test seems to be related to the source VM not having an IPv6 address or routes post-migration. This is crucial for maintaining network connectivity between the VMs.

Here are a few things you might want to check or try:

1. **Passt Binding Plugin Limitations**: The Passt binding plugin is currently in the Alpha stage and has some limitations, such as not supporting custom CIDR configurations in the guest and secondary networks <sup>[[1]](https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/network/net_binding_plugins/passt)</sup>. These limitations might affect the IPv6 configuration during migration.

2. **Network Configuration**: Ensure that the network configuration for the VMs includes proper IPv6 setup. The Passt plugin should be configured to handle IPv6 addresses and routes correctly. Verify that the `NetworkBindingPlugins` feature gate is enabled in the KubeVirt configuration, as this is necessary for the Passt plugin to function <sup>[[2]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/cmd/sidecars/network-passt-binding/README.md)</sup>.

3. **Migration Process**: During migration, KubeVirt should preserve the network configuration, including IPv6 addresses. Check if the migration process is correctly handling the IPv6 setup by ensuring that the `FindMigrationIP` function is retrieving a global unicast IPv6 address for the migration network interface <sup>[[3]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/pkg/virt-handler/migration.go)</sup>.

4. **Logs and Debugging**: Check the logs for any error messages or warnings related to the Passt binding plugin during the migration. The Passt log file path is set to `/var/run/kubevirt/passt.log`, which might provide more context on the issue <sup>[[4]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/tests/network/bindingplugin_passt.go)</sup>.

By addressing these areas, you might be able to resolve the issue with the IPv6 configuration during the migration test.

In KubeVirt v1.5.0, the removal of the privileged security profile affects the ability to change file ownership in virtiofs mounts. The virtiofsd daemon runs with the QEMU UID/GID (107) and cannot switch between different UIDs/GIDs. Therefore, it will only have access to directories and files that UID/GID 107 has permission to. When creating new files, they will always be created with QEMU's UID/GID regardless of the UID/GID of the process within the guest <sup>[[1]](https://kubevirt.io/user-guide/storage/disks_and_volumes)</sup>.

To work around this limitation, you can ensure that the directories and files you need to access are owned by UID/GID 107 or have appropriate permissions set to allow access by this UID/GID. Alternatively, you might consider using a different method for file sharing that allows for more flexible ownership management, such as using a different type of volume or storage solution that supports changing ownership.

In your situation, since you don't have access to the host to change the ownership of the PVC, and given the constraints of virtiofs in KubeVirt v1.5.0, you might consider the following approaches:

1. **Use a Kubernetes Job or Init Container**: You can create a Kubernetes Job or use an Init Container in your VMI to change the ownership of the files within the PVC to the `qemu` user (UID 107) before the VMI starts. This way, the virtiofsd daemon will have the necessary permissions to access the files.

2. **Set Permissions on PVC Creation**: If possible, modify the process that creates the PVC to set the appropriate permissions and ownership at creation time. This might involve using a custom script or tool that sets the ownership to UID 107.

3. **Alternative Storage Solutions**: Consider using a different storage solution that allows for more flexible ownership management. For example, NFS or other network-based storage solutions might provide the flexibility you need.

These approaches can help you work around the limitations imposed by the virtiofs security constraints in KubeVirt v1.5.0.

This symbol is part of the internal GLIBC interface and is not meant to be used directly by applications.

Here are a few steps you can take to troubleshoot and potentially resolve this issue:

1. **Check GLIBC Version**: Ensure that the GLIBC version on your system is compatible with the libraries you are linking against. The error might be due to a mismatch between the GLIBC version used to compile the libraries and the one present on your system.

2. **Update Dependencies**: Make sure all your dependencies are up to date. This includes the system libraries and any specific libraries required by KubeVirt. You can try updating your system packages and re-running `make rpm-deps`.

3. **Cross-Compilation Configuration**: Verify that the cross-compilation setup for Arm64 is correctly configured. The `cc_toolchain_config.bzl` file should specify the correct paths and flags for the Arm64 architecture <sup>[[1]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/bazel/toolchain/aarch64-none-linux-gnu/cc_toolchain_config.bzl)</sup>.

4. **Bazel Configuration**: Check the `BUILD.bazel` file for any architecture-specific configurations that might need adjustment for Arm64. Ensure that the dependencies and configurations are correctly specified for Arm64 <sup>[[2]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/BUILD.bazel)</sup>.

5. **Sandbox Debugging**: Use the `--sandbox_debug` flag with Bazel to get more detailed output, which might help identify the root cause of the linking issue.

6. **Rebuild from Scratch**: Sometimes, cleaning the build environment and starting from scratch can resolve issues. You can try running `bazel clean` before attempting the build again.

If these steps do not resolve the issue, you may need to investigate further into the specific versions of the libraries and toolchains being used in your environment.

The error message you're encountering, "Cannot find CPU model with PVR 0xd0b," suggests that there is an issue with CPU model detection on your Raspberry Pi 5 cluster. KubeVirt sets the default CPU model to "host-passthrough" for ARM64 architecture, which should help in maintaining compatibility by using the host's CPU model <sup>[[1]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/pkg/defaults/arm64.go)</sup>.

Here are a few steps you can try to resolve the issue:

1. **Verify CPU Model Configuration**: Ensure that the CPU model is set to "host-passthrough" in your VirtualMachineInstance (VMI) specification. This setting allows the VM to use the host's CPU model, which is crucial for compatibility on ARM devices.

2. **Check KubeVirt and Libvirt Versions**: Make sure that both KubeVirt and libvirt are up-to-date and compatible with your Raspberry Pi 5 hardware. Sometimes, newer versions include fixes for specific hardware compatibility issues.

3. **Review Logs for Additional Clues**: Check the logs for both KubeVirt and libvirt for any additional error messages or warnings that might provide more context about the issue.

4. **Consult ARM-Specific Documentation**: Although specific documentation for Raspberry Pi 5 might not be available, reviewing ARM-specific sections in the KubeVirt documentation could provide insights into any additional configurations required.

If these steps do not resolve the issue, it might be worth checking if there are any known issues or discussions in the KubeVirt community regarding Raspberry Pi 5 compatibility.

The "Paused(3):IOError(5)" status you're encountering indicates an I/O error, which is causing the VM to pause automatically. This can happen due to several reasons, such as storage issues, network interruptions, or resource constraints.

Here are some steps you can take to troubleshoot and resolve this issue:

1. **Check Storage and Network**: Ensure that the storage backend used by the VM is stable and has no connectivity issues. Similarly, verify that there are no network interruptions affecting the VM's operation.

2. **Resource Allocation**: Although your VM is configured with 4 CPUs and 16 GiB of memory, ensure that the underlying Kubernetes nodes have sufficient resources to support this configuration. Overcommitting resources can lead to unexpected behavior.

3. **Disk Space and I/O Performance**: Check if there is sufficient disk space available and that the I/O performance is adequate for the VM's workload. High I/O latency or disk space exhaustion can lead to pausing.

4. **Logs and Events**: Review the logs and events from the `virt-launcher` pod and the Kubernetes node hosting the VM for any additional error messages or warnings that might provide more context.

5. **Migration Settings**: If the VM is part of a migration process, ensure that the migration settings are configured correctly to avoid pausing due to migration timeouts or bandwidth limitations.

If the issue persists after these checks, consider restarting the VM as a temporary workaround, as you've mentioned it resolves the issue. However, identifying and addressing the root cause is crucial to prevent recurrence.

I found a similar closed issue regarding macvtap errors, but no solution was found in the comments <sup>[[1]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/11031)</sup>.

In KubeVirt v1.5.0, the ownership and permissions for `/dev/tap*` devices are determined by the `AddTapDevice` and `AddTapDeviceWithSELinuxLabel` methods in the `VirtCHRoot` struct. These methods set the user ID and group ID for the tap device using the `ownerID` provided to the method <sup>[[2]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/pkg/network/driver/virtchroot/tap.go)</sup>.

Additionally, there is a configuration option `device_ownership_from_security_context` in KubeVirt v1.5.0 that affects device permissions. This option should be set in your Container Runtime Interface (CRI) configuration to handle block device ownership properly and resolve permission issues. Here are the configurations for different CRIs:

For Containerd v1:
```toml
[plugins]
    [plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri"]
      device_ownership_from_security_context = true
```

For Containerd v2:
```toml
[plugins]
    [plugins."io.containerd.cri.v1.runtime"]
      device_ownership_from_security_context = true
```

For CRI-O:
```toml
[crio.runtime]
device_ownership_from_security_context = true
```
<sup>[[3]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/issues/14335)</sup>.

These configurations might help resolve the permission issues you're experiencing with macvtap interfaces in KubeVirt v1.5.0.

**What happened**:

During peak hours, there was a burst of VMI deletions and creations. With around 2500 VMIs in the cluster, 200 VMIs were deleted and re-created.

This lead to larger vmiCreationToRunning times. Upon investigating, it was found that virt-controller was being slow because of client side rate limiter that needs to get the network-attachment-devices.

This function call is in the critical path of vmiCreationToRunning, because for each vmi, virt-controller looks up the networkMap to render the virt-launcher pod manifest [here](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/98adfe88a94816a9381c3442372e80e067b98acc/pkg/virt-controller/services/template.go#L375) and [here](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/98adfe88a94816a9381c3442372e80e067b98acc/pkg/network/multus/nad.go#L64) 

**What you expected to happen**:

virt-controller should to make a cached informer get call to NetworkAttachDefinitions, instead of going to apiserver directly

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
1. Have a really small qps and burst configuration in kubevirt CR, for example qps of 5 and burst of 10
2. Using the perf/scale stack, create 100 fake nodes and 1000 fake VMIs that use more than 1 network
3. logs similar to the following will will appear:
```

To resolve the issue with `git describe` returning an abbreviated commit hash prefixed by `-g`, you can modify the `generate.sh` script to strip the `-g` prefix from the version string. This can be done by using a command like `sed` to process the output of `git describe`. Here is an example modification to the script:

```sh
# Define version of client
if [ -n "${DOCKER_TAG:-}" ]; then
    CLIENT_PYTHON_VERSION="$DOCKER_TAG"
else
    CLIENT_PYTHON_VERSION="$(git describe --tags --always | sed 's/-g//')"
fi
```

Additionally, you can refer to the `hack/version.sh` script from the KubeVirt repository, which provides a more comprehensive approach to handling version strings. This script uses `sed` to transform the output of `git describe` into a semantic version format, ensuring compatibility with setuptools requirements. Specifically, it replaces the `-g` prefix with a `+` sign for the commit hash, which aligns with semantic versioning practices:

```bash
if [[ "${DASHES_IN_VERSION}" == "--" ]]; then
    # We have distance to base tag (v1.1.0-1-gCommitHash)
    KUBEVIRT_GIT_VERSION=$(echo "${KUBEVIRT_GIT_VERSION}" | sed "s/-g\([0-9a-f]\{14\}\)$/+\1/")
fi
```

This approach ensures that the version string is both semantically correct and compatible with setuptools <sup>[[1]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/hack/gen-client-python/generate.sh)</sup><sup>[[2]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/hack/version.sh)</sup>.

The virt-handler in KubeVirt specifies the cgroup range for Unix98 PTY clients from `c 136:-1` to `c 151:-1` because it includes 16 major numbers starting from 136. This is implemented in the code as follows:

```go
const ptyFirstMajor int64 = 136
const ptyMajors int64 = 16

for i := int64(0); i < ptyMajors; i++ {
    defaultRules = append(defaultRules,
        &devices.Rule{
            Type:        devices.CharDevice,
            Major:       ptyFirstMajor + i,
            Minor:       -1,
            Permissions: permissions,
            Allow:       toAllow,
        })
}
```

This loop iterates 16 times, resulting in the range from 136 to 151. While this differs from the Linux documentation, which specifies the range as `c 136:-1` to `c 143:-1`, the implementation in KubeVirt is consistent with the logic in the code <sup>[[1]](https://github.com/kubevirt/kubevirt/blob/main/pkg/virt-handler/cgroup/util.go)</sup>.
